231.event_title: Sir Thomas Bodley reopens Oxford's university library
231.event: Oxford's old university library had been stripped of its books and furniture in the mid-sixteenth century. The retired diplomat Thomas Bodley offered to restore it, personally paying for and directing its refurbishment from 1598 and giving books of his own, and the library opened on 8 November 1602. In 1610 he secured an agreement under which the Stationers' Company would give the library a copy of every book printed in England.
231.explanation: A private fortune given to a public institution made Bodley's name permanent: the library has been called the Bodleian ever since.
231.tie_back: The kural says the only real profit of life is to give and to live so that praise gathers around one's name, and Bodley's gift turned his wealth into a name that has lasted four centuries.
231._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of giving that produced lasting renown, though the gift was to an institution rather than directly to the poor, as the classical commentary specifies.

232.event_title: Maecenas becomes the patron of Virgil and Horace
232.event: Gaius Maecenas, a wealthy adviser to Augustus who remained an equestrian and never held high office, supported a circle of poets that included Virgil and Horace. Virgil dedicated the Georgics to him, Horace dedicated several works to him, and Maecenas gave Horace an estate in the Sabine hills. His name became proverbial for a generous patron of the arts.
232.explanation: The praise of the greatest poets of the age settled on the man who supported them, so lastingly that his name became a common word for a patron.
232.tie_back: The kural says that all the praise that poets utter comes to rest on those who give, and in Maecenas the poets' praise literally became the giver's name.
232._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: the bardic praise described in the commentary settled on a patron so completely that his name became a byword.

233.event_title: James Prinsep deciphers the edicts of Ashoka
233.event: Before the 1830s the Mauryan emperor Ashoka was known almost only from Buddhist chronicles. In 1837 the British scholar James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script of inscriptions on pillars and rocks, revealing edicts issued by a king who called himself Beloved of the Gods, Piyadasi. These edicts were identified as Ashoka's, restoring a major ruler to history after some two thousand years.
233.explanation: An emperor whose empire, cities and dynasty had all vanished was brought back to the world's memory through the record of his moral teaching carved in stone.
233.tie_back: The kural says nothing in this world stands except exalted renown, and Ashoka's palaces perished while the edicts recording his ideals survived to restore his name.
233._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Ashoka's name survived through his recorded deeds, though it had in fact been largely forgotten until Prinsep's work, which complicates the claim of unbroken renown.

234.event_title: Yuri Gagarin's world tour after the first human spaceflight
234.place: Moscow, Soviet Union, and cities around the world
234.event: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space, orbiting the Earth once in Vostok 1. Two days later he appeared beside Premier Khrushchev in Moscow, and he then made a worldwide tour, greeted by cheering crowds; in July 1961 he visited London and Manchester at the invitation of a trade union, meeting dignitaries and royalty, and he also met India's Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
234.explanation: At the height of the Cold War, a single achievement made one man's name celebrated across rival blocs and continents.
234.tie_back: The kural speaks of renown that reaches the ends of the earth and is honoured even above the celestials, and Gagarin, who had himself gone beyond the sky, was acclaimed across the whole globe.
234._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shows renown reaching the ends of the earth, but the kural's claim that heaven honours such a person over its own sages has no historical counterpart.

235.event_title: Joan of Arc is executed, rehabilitated and canonised
235.event: Joan of Arc, the peasant girl who led French forces to relieve Orleans during the Hundred Years' War, was tried by an ecclesiastical court and executed at Rouen on 30 May 1431. On the order of Pope Callixtus III, proceedings in 1455-56 annulled her conviction, and in 1920 she was canonised by Pope Benedict XV, while the French parliament decreed a yearly national festival in her honour.
235.explanation: A death meant to discredit her became the foundation of a renown that has grown for nearly six centuries; she is honoured as France's national heroine and patron saint.
235.tie_back: The kural speaks of a death that is really a way of living on, and Joan's execution became the beginning of her enduring life in the memory of her nation.
235._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the kural's paradox of a death that becomes lasting life through renown.

236.event_title: Abebe Bikila wins the Olympic marathon barefoot
236.event: Abebe Bikila, a late addition to Ethiopia's team, ran the Rome Olympic marathon barefoot and won in a world-best time of 2 hours 15 minutes 16.2 seconds. He became the first Black African to win an Olympic gold medal, and in Tokyo in 1964 he became the first person to win two Olympic marathons.
236.explanation: Bikila's first appearance on the world stage was so distinguished that it changed how the world saw African athletes.
236.tie_back: The kural says that whoever appears before the world should appear with qualities that bring renown, and Bikila's first Olympic appearance did exactly that.
236._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the vocational reading of the kural (entering a field with distinction), less so of the existential reading about birth.

237.event_title: President Kennedy takes responsibility for the Bay of Pigs
237.event: In April 1961 an invasion of Cuba by CIA-trained Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs failed within days. At his news conference on 21 April, President John F. Kennedy, pressed about the failure, noted the old saying that victory has a hundred fathers and defeat is an orphan, and stated that he was the responsible officer of the government. His public approval rating rose to 83 percent in the weeks that followed.
237.explanation: Instead of blaming advisers, agencies or critics, Kennedy publicly owned the failure, and the public respected him for it.
237.tie_back: The kural asks why those who fall short resent their critics instead of grieving over themselves, and Kennedy answered a defeat by taking the blame on himself.
237._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of accepting responsibility rather than blaming others; the kural's emphasis on self-reproach is matched in public, though Kennedy's private feelings are not part of the event.

238.event_title: James Smithson's bequest founds the Smithsonian Institution
238.place: London, England, and Washington, D.C., United States
238.event: James Smithson, a British scientist and the illegitimate son of Hugh Smithson, 1st Duke of Northumberland, never visited the United States and had no children. His will of 1826 provided that if his nephew died without heirs, his estate should go to the United States to found at Washington an institution bearing his name for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. The nephew died childless in 1835, Congress accepted the gift in 1836, and the Smithsonian Institution was established by an Act signed on 10 August 1846.
238.explanation: A childless man denied his father's name left a legacy that made his own name one of the best known in the world of learning.
238.tie_back: The kural calls renown the legacy every life should leave behind, and Smithson, with no children, left a name that has outlived any line of descendants.
238._accuracy_note: A strong fit with the kural's image of renown as one's true offspring, though Smithson's own motives are undocumented.

239.event_title: Norman Borlaug's wheat transforms harvests in Mexico and South Asia
239.event: From 1944 Norman Borlaug worked on a Rockefeller Foundation programme in Mexico, where he developed high-yielding, disease-resistant wheat varieties, and Mexico became self-sufficient in wheat in 1956. In the 1960s these varieties were introduced to India and Pakistan, where wheat yields nearly doubled between 1965 and 1970. Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
239.explanation: The work of one renowned scientist and his colleagues changed the yield of whole countries' land and averted famines that had been widely predicted.
239.tie_back: The kural says the land bearing a person without renown sees its harvest decline; Borlaug shows the converse, a person of lasting renown under whose work the land's yield multiplied.
239._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the kural's claim of a moral link between a person's renown and the fertility of the soil cannot be illustrated literally, so this shows the converse in a practical sense.

240.event_title: Socrates refuses to escape before his execution
240.event: In 399 BCE Socrates was tried in Athens on charges of impiety and corrupting the young, convicted and sentenced to death. While he awaited execution, his friend Crito urged him to escape into exile, which was a realistic option, but Socrates refused, arguing that escape would be a wrong against the laws he had lived under. He drank the poison, most likely hemlock, and died calmly among his friends.
240.explanation: Socrates chose a blameless death over a compromised life, and his example has been treated ever since as a model of integrity.
240.tie_back: The kural says that only those who live free of reproach truly live, and Socrates judged that a life bought by doing wrong would not be worth living.
240._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of valuing blamelessness above mere survival, though the details come chiefly from Plato's accounts.
